name: Maxwell's Equations
statement: Four coupled equations describe how electric and magnetic fields are generated by charges, currents, and each other's rate of change.
statementAccent: electric and magnetic fields are generated by charges, currents, and each other's rate of change
meaning: Maxwell's equations unify electricity, magnetism, and optics into a single field theory. They show that a changing magnetic field creates an electric field (Faraday's law) and a changing electric field, together with current, creates a magnetic field (the Ampère–Maxwell law), while the two Gauss's laws describe how field lines relate to charge and the absence of magnetic monopoles.
mechanism: The equations are local differential relationships between the electric field, magnetic field, charge density, and current density, drawn from Coulomb’s, Ampère’s, and Faraday’s laws, with Maxwell adding a "displacement current" term to make the system self-consistent. Combining them yields a wave equation whose propagation speed equals the speed of light, showing that light itself is an electromagnetic wave.

examples.text: Maxwell’s 1865 paper "A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field" derived a wave equation whose calculated speed matched the known speed of light, leading him to conclude light is an electromagnetic wave.

Maxwell’s original 1865 paper contained twenty equations; in 1884 Oliver Heaviside, with related work by Josiah Willard Gibbs and Heinrich Hertz, condensed them into the four vector equations taught today.
The prediction of propagating electromagnetic waves underlies radio, radar, and wireless communication, all of which rely on generating and detecting oscillating electric and magnetic fields.

whyItMatters: Maxwell’s equations are the foundation of classical electromagnetism, underpinning virtually all electrical, electronic, and optical technology. They also represent one of the first successful field-theoretic unifications in physics, foreshadowing special relativity.
limits: The equations are classical (non-quantum) and break down at scales requiring quantum electrodynamics. They also assume a given spacetime geometry unless coupled with general relativity in curved-spacetime formulations.
misreadings: They are often misattributed as all four having been written by Maxwell in vector form; in fact Maxwell used component/quaternion notation, and the compact four-equation vector version is Heaviside’s reformulation.
origin: Formulated by James Clerk Maxwell, published 1861–1862 and consolidated in his 1865 paper; the modern four-equation form was produced by Oliver Heaviside in 1884.
